name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
principle: The code allocates or retains a limited resource without hard bounds or throttling. An attacker can drive the process, host, or dependent service into exhaustion, causing denial of service and sometimes fail-open behavior.
detection_signals: attacker-controlled size/count passed to `malloc`, `new`, `ByteBuffer.allocate`, `ArrayList.add`, or similar with no max check
`while(true)`, `for(;;)`, or retry loops driven by input/network events with no termination or budget
`accept()` / request handler that creates a new `Thread`, `fork()`, or task per connection without a bounded pool
reads from socket/file into memory or disk until EOF with no quota, cap, or total-bytes counter
cache, queue, map, log, or buffer grows on each request with no eviction, size limit, or backpressure
expensive work on each request with no rate limiter, semaphore, or concurrency cap
negative_signals: explicit hard cap such as `if (n > MAX_N) reject();` before allocation or enqueue
bounded executor or pool, e.g. fixed thread pool or bounded queue with reject policy
token bucket, rate limiter, or semaphore guarding the expensive path
fixed-size buffers or preallocated pools with no attacker-driven growth
cache/log rotation or eviction policy with explicit size or entry limit
safe failure path on pressure, e.g. reject request and release resources immediately
false_defense_traps: `catch (OutOfMemoryError)` or generic exception handling without limiting the source of consumption
`sleep()` or artificial delay after each request instead of a hard concurrency/rate cap
relying only on OS/container limits while the application still allocates without bounds
validating payload type/format but not the maximum count, length, or lifetime
limiting per-request size while total concurrent requests, threads, or queued items remain unbounded
verification_focus: Is every attacker-influenced allocation, loop, queue, thread/process spawn, or cache growth bounded by a hard limit or throttle?

consequence_chains.trigger: attacker-controlled size or count reaches an allocation, spawn, or queue operation with no maximum
consequence_chains.consequence: CPU, memory, or descriptor exhaustion leading to denial of service

consequence_chains.trigger: repeated creation of resources without tracking, reuse, or release
consequence_chains.consequence: resource leak accumulates until the process or host becomes unavailable

patch_principle: Add hard limits on count, size, duration, and concurrency before any expensive operation
Use bounded pools, bounded queues, and explicit rejection/backpressure for overflow
Apply per-user, per-IP, or per-session rate limits and quotas at the entry point
Fail closed under resource pressure and release resources promptly in all paths
